extracted.intended_audience: High school students taking the SAT (School Day) and their educators/counselors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and scoring rubric for the SAT Essay administered on SAT School Day: what the essay asks students to do, the characteristics of source passages, timing and format, and the three-dimension scoring rubric (Reading, Analysis, Writing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures comprehension of the passage, including interplay of central ideas and important details, and effective use of textual evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scored 1–4. 4 (Advanced): demonstrates thorough comprehension; shows understanding of central idea(s) and most important details and how they interrelate; free of errors of fact or interpretation; makes skillful use of textual evidence (quotations, paraphrases, or both), demonstrating a complete understanding of the source text. 3 (Proficient): demonstrates effective comprehension; understands central idea(s) and important details; free of substantive errors of fact and interpretation; makes appropriate use of textual evidence demonstrating understanding. 2 (Partial): demonstrates some comprehension; shows understanding of central idea(s) but not important details; may contain errors of fact/interpretation; makes limited and/or haphazard use of textual evidence. 1 (Inadequate): demonstrates little or no comprehension; fails to show understanding of central idea(s); may include only details without reference to central ideas; may contain numerous errors of fact/interpretation; makes little or no use of textual evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures understanding of how the author builds an argument by examining use of evidence, reasoning, and/or stylistic and persuasive techniques and supporting claims effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scored 1–4. 4 (Advanced): offers an insightful analysis and demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of the analytical task; offers a thorough, well-considered evaluation of the author's use of evidence, reasoning, and/or stylistic and persuasive elements (and/or feature(s) of student's choice); contains relevant, sufficient, and strategically chosen support for claims; focuses consistently on features most relevant to the task. 3 (Proficient): offers an effective analysis and demonstrates understanding of the analytical task; competently evaluates the author's use of evidence, reasoning, and/or stylistic/persuasive elements (and/or feature(s) of student's choice); contains relevant and sufficient support for claims; focuses primarily on features most relevant to the task. 2 (Partial): offers limited analysis and demonstrates only partial understanding of the analytical task; identifies and attempts to describe the author's use of evidence/reasoning/stylistic elements but merely asserts rather than explains their importance, or has unwarranted aspects; contains little or no support for claims; may lack clear focus on most relevant features. 1 (Inadequate): offers little or no analysis or ineffective analysis and demonstrates little or no understanding of the analytical task; identifies without explanation some aspects of the author's use of evidence/reasoning/stylistic elements, or numerous aspects of analysis are unwarranted; contains little or no support for claims or support is largely irrelevant; may offer no discernible analysis (largely summary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures cohesion, organization, precision, appropriate style and tone, sentence variety, and conventions of standard written English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scored 1–4. 4 (Advanced): response is cohesive and demonstrates a highly effective use and command of language; includes a precise central claim, skillful introduction and conclusion; demonstrates deliberate and highly effective progression of ideas both within paragraphs and throughout; wide variety in sentence structures; consistent use of precise word choice; maintains a formal style and objective tone; shows strong command of conventions and is free or virtually free of errors. 3 (Proficient): mostly cohesive and demonstrates effective use and control of language; includes a central claim or implicit controlling idea and an effective introduction and conclusion; demonstrates a clear progression of ideas within and throughout the essay; variety in sentence structures; some precise word choice; maintains formal style and objective tone; good control of conventions and free of significant errors that detract. 2 (Partial): little or no cohesion and limited skill in use/control of language; may lack clear central claim or deviate from claim; may include ineffective introduction/conclusion; may demonstrate progression within paragraphs but not throughout; limited variety in sentence structures; general or vague word choice; may deviate from formal style; limited control of conventions and contains errors that detract and may impede understanding. 1 (Inadequate): little or no cohesion and inadequate skill in language; may lack central claim, recognizable introduction/conclusion, or progression of ideas; lacks variety in sentence structures; poor or inaccurate word choice; lacks formal style and objective tone; weak control of conventions and may contain numerous errors that undermine quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essay Prompt Requirements (task instructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: What the student is asked to do in the prompt: read the passage and explain how the author builds an argument to persuade an audience, analyzing specific features and supporting the explanation with evidence from the passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt directs students to consider how the author uses: evidence (facts/examples) to support claims; reasoning to develop ideas and connect claims and evidence; stylistic or persuasive elements (word choice, appeals to emotion) to add power. Students should write an essay explaining how the author builds an argument to persuade the audience, analyzing one or more of the listed features (or other chosen features) to strengthen the logic and persuasiveness of the argument. The analysis should focus on the most relevant features. Students should not state whether they agree with the author’s claims, but should explain how the author builds the argument. The prompt includes points to consider and directions; the actual test prompt will be nearly identical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essay Passage Characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Common properties of source passages used on the SAT Essay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All passages are written for a broad audience, argue a point, express subtle views on complex subjects, use logical reasoning and evidence to support claims, and examine ideas/debates/trends in the arts and sciences or in civic, cultural, or political life. All passages are taken from published works. The page notes: 'All the information you need to write your essay will be included in the passage or in notes about it.' Use these characteristics when deciding what features to analyze and which textual evidence is relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test Format and Timing (essay logistics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural and timing constraints for the SAT Essay on SAT School Day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overview: Total questions — 1 prompt with points to consider and directions; 1 passage. Time allotted — 50 minutes to read, analyze the passage, and develop a written response. The Essay is only available in certain states where required as part of SAT School Day administrations; students should check with their counselor whether their administration includes the Essay. Practice materials and scored samples are available via Bluebook and My Practice.
